nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the short-story writer of Guests of the Nation and the critic of the short story
literary_identity: Short-story writer, poet and critic; the author of Guests of the Nation and of the theory of the short story.
biography: Born Michael Francis O'Connor O'Donovan at Cork on 17 September 1903; he fought on the anti-Treaty side in the civil war and was interned, and published the stories of Guests of the Nation in 1931 and Bones of Contention in 1936. As librarian, teacher and critic - The Lonely Voice (1963) is the theory of the short story - and as translator of the Irish verse, he made the Irish short story one of the forms of the century; he died in Dublin on 10 March 1966.
literary_profile: Frank O'Connor is one of the two or three masters of the Irish short story: Guests of the Nation put the civil war and the ordinary decencies into the form, Bones of Contention carried the Cork of his childhood into the story, and The Lonely Voice gave the short story its theory of the submerged population.
stylistic_characteristics: The short story of the single moral turn told in the spoken Irish-English; the Cork of the childhood and the civil war; the plain sentence of the teller who reports the decencies; the translation that carries the Irish verse into English; the criticism of the form as the art of the submerged.
intellectual_concerns: The civil war and the internment camp; the Irish short story and its submerged population; Cork and the childhood; the Irish verse and its translation; the ordinary decencies against the ideology.
historical_significance: Frank O'Connor is one of the masters of the Irish short story: Guests of the Nation put the civil war into the form, and The Lonely Voice gave the short story its theory of the submerged population.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the short-story writer, the novelist of Bird Alone and the editor of The Bell
literary_identity: Short-story writer, novelist, critic and editor; the founder of The Bell and the biographer of the revival.
biography: Born Sean Proinsias O Faolain at Cork on 22 February 1900; he fought in the IRA and the civil war, and published Midsummer Night Madness (1932), The Saint and Mary Kate (1932) and Bird Alone (1936). As editor of The Bell from 1940 and as critic and biographer of the revival he shaped Irish letters for two decades; he died at Dublin on 20 April 1991.
literary_profile: Sean O'Faolain is the central figure of Irish letters between the war and the republic: Midsummer Night Madness and Bird Alone made the short story and the novel of the civil war and the censorship, The Bell gave Irish writing its magazine for the 1940s, and his criticism of the revival fixed the terms of the national question in literature.
stylistic_characteristics: The short story of the civil war and the censorship in the plain ironic sentence; the novel of the young man against the church and the state; the criticism of the revival as the argument with the fathers; the editor's prose of the standard and the quarrel; the biography of the national leader as the study of the myth.
intellectual_concerns: The civil war and the republic that followed; the censorship and the church; the Irish short story and its magazine; the revival and the argument with the fathers; the national question as the question of the writer.
historical_significance: Sean O'Faolain is the central figure of Irish letters between the war and the republic: Bird Alone and Midsummer Night Madness made the fiction of the civil war and the censorship, and The Bell gave Irish writing its magazine of the 1940s.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the novelist of the Irish middle class, the convent and the censored book
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of Without My Cloak, Mary Lavelle and The Last of Summer.
biography: Born Kate O'Brien at Limerick on 23 July 1897; she worked as a governess and a journalist before Without My Cloak (1931) won the James Tait Black prize. The Anteroom (1934), Mary Lavelle (1936) - banned in Ireland - and The Last of Summer (1943) made her the novelist of the Irish middle class, the convent and the censored desire; she died at Faversham, Kent, on 13 August 1974.
literary_profile: Kate O'Brien is the novelist of the Irish middle class and of the censored conscience: Without My Cloak made the Limerick family a chronicle of the century, Mary Lavelle carried the convent-bred woman into the forbidden love that the Irish state banned, and The Last of Summer is the finest of her novels of the return to Ireland.
stylistic_characteristics: The prose of the family chronicle and the censored conscience; the Limerick middle class and the convent; the woman's desire stated plainly against the church and the state; the return to Ireland as the novel's occasion; the dialogue of the drawing room and the chapel.
intellectual_concerns: The Irish middle class and the family chronicle; the convent, the church and the censored book; the woman's desire and the marriage question; exile and the return to Ireland; the censorship as the subject of the novel.
historical_significance: Kate O'Brien is the novelist of the Irish middle class and of the censored conscience: Without My Cloak made the Limerick family a chronicle, Mary Lavelle carried the censored desire into the canon, and The Last of Summer is the finest of her novels of the return.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the big-house novelist and satirist of the Anglo-Irish, as M. J. Farrell
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; 'M. J. Farrell', the satirist of the Anglo-Irish big house.
biography: Born Mary Nesta Skrine at Newbridge, County Kildare, on 20 July 1904, the daughter of the poet Moira O'Neill; she published eight novels as M. J. Farrell from The Knight of Cheerful Countenance (1926) to The Rising Tide (1937), with the comedy Spring Meeting (1938, with John Perry) beside them, and returned after the war as Molly Keane with Good Behaviour (1949) and the late masterpieces. She died at Ardmore, County Waterford, on 22 April 1996.
literary_profile: Molly Keane is the satirist of the Anglo-Irish big house: the Farrell novels of the 1920s and 1930s dissected the vicious snobbery of her own class with the affection of the insider, and the return as Molly Keane made the big-house novel one of the forms of the Irish twentieth century.
stylistic_characteristics: The satirical sentence of the insider; the big house, the hunt and the drawing room of the Anglo-Irish; the dialogue of the class that cannot see itself; the comedy of manners turned to the elegy of the house; the later first-person of the unloved daughter.
intellectual_concerns: The Anglo-Irish big house and its decay; the snobbery and the genteel racism of the class; the hunt, the dinner and the drawing room; the woman of the house and the unloved daughter; the comedy of manners as the elegy of a class.
historical_significance: Molly Keane is the satirist of the Anglo-Irish big house: the Farrell novels dissected her own class with the affection of the insider, and the return as Molly Keane made the big-house novel one of the forms of the Irish twentieth century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the early prose and verse of Murphy and the Joyce essay
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and critic; the author of More Pricks Than Kicks, Echo's Bones and Murphy before the war.
biography: Born Samuel Barclay Beckett at Foxrock, Dublin, on 13 April 1906; he read Romance languages at Trinity College Dublin and taught in Paris, where the essay 'Dante...Bruno. Vico..Joyce' (1929) placed him in the Joyce circle. More Pricks Than Kicks (1934), Echo's Bones and Other Precipitates (1935) and Murphy (1938) are the Dublin and London books of the 1930s; the war, the Resistance and the French trilogy followed. He received the Nobel prize in 1969 and died in Paris on 22 December 1989.
literary_profile: Samuel Beckett is the central writer of the twentieth century and his English books of the 1930s are the first act of it: the Joyce essay stated the poetics of the wake, More Pricks Than Kicks and Echo's Bones gave the comic elegy of Belacqua, and Murphy is the novel of the mind in the body that the later prose would dissolve.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic elegiac sentence of the learned allusion and the bodily joke; the paralysis of the will as the plot; the Dublin and London of the young intellectual; the verse of the precipitate and the echo; the prose that thinks against its own speaker.
intellectual_concerns: The mind and the body and the little world of the former; Joyce and the poetics of the wake; the comic and the elegiac in the same sentence; paralysis and the refusal of the will; the war and the Resistance as the break of the career.
historical_significance: Samuel Beckett is the central writer of the twentieth century: the English books of the 1930s - the Joyce essay, More Pricks Than Kicks, Echo's Bones and Murphy - are the first act of the career that the French trilogy and the plays would complete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the experimental novelist of At Swim-Two-Birds and the columnist Cruiskeen Lawn
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and columnist; 'Myles na gCopaleen', the author of At Swim-Two-Birds.
biography: Born Brian O'Nolan at Strabane, County Tyrone, on 5 April 1911; he entered the Irish civil service and published At Swim-Two-Birds in 1939, the experimental novel of the author and his characters. As 'Myles na gCopaleen' he wrote the Cruiskeen Lawn column in The Irish Times from 1940 and the Abbey play Faustus Kelly (1943); The Third Policeman, written in the war years, was published only after his death. He died in Dublin on 1 April 1966.
literary_profile: Flann O'Brien is the great experimental comic novelist of Ireland: At Swim-Two-Birds made the novel of the author and his characters the form of the Irish modernism, the Cruiskeen Lawn column is the finest comic journalism in Irish English, and The Third Policeman, written in the war years, is the comic metaphysic of the police and the bicycle.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic metaphysic carried in the deadpan of the civil servant; the novel of the author and his characters in several hands; the column of the pseudonym, the gloss and the learned joke; the Irish-English of the office and the pub; the bicycle, the police and the third place.
intellectual_concerns: The novel as the game of the author and his characters; the Irish civil service and the office; the pseudonym and the column; the comic metaphysic of the thing and the person; the Irish language and the Gaelic joke of Myles.
historical_significance: Flann O'Brien is the great experimental comic novelist of Ireland: At Swim-Two-Birds made the novel of the author and his characters the form of the Irish modernism, and the Cruiskeen Lawn column is the finest comic journalism in Irish English.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Monaghan poet of The Great Hunger and the ploughman
literary_identity: Poet; the Monaghan ploughman-poet of The Great Hunger.
biography: Born Patrick Kavanagh at Inniskeen, County Monaghan, on 21 October 1904, the son of a small farmer and shoemaker; he farmed the stony land until The Ploughman and Other Poems (1936) and the autobiography The Green Fool (1938) made him a writer in Dublin. The Great Hunger (1942), the long poem of the clay and the celibate farmer, is his masterpiece; he died in Dublin on 30 November 1967.
literary_profile: Patrick Kavanagh is the Monaghan poet of the Irish twentieth century: The Great Hunger made the clay, the potato and the celibate farmer the matter of the long poem and answered the Ireland of the revival with the Ireland of the parish, and his lyrics of the ploughman are the plain voice of the small farm.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain line of the ploughman's speech charged with the clay; the long poem of the parish and the celibate; the lyric of the field, the ass and the fair; the quarrel with the Ireland of the revival and the folklore; the prose of the country boy in the city.
intellectual_concerns: The parish and the clay of Monaghan; the great hunger of the land and of the body; the celibacy of the small farmer; the quarrel with the literary Ireland of Dublin; the commonplace as the sacred.
historical_significance: Patrick Kavanagh is the Monaghan poet of the Irish twentieth century: The Great Hunger made the clay and the celibate farmer the matter of the long poem and answered the Ireland of the revival with the Ireland of the parish.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the symbolist lyric, the verse play and the poetry of the national revival
literary_identity: Poet and dramatist; the founder of the Irish Literary Revival, the greatest poet in English of the period's first half, and the Nobel laureate of 1923.
biography: Born William Butler Yeats in Sandymount, Dublin, on 13 June 1865, the son of the painter John Butler Yeats; he was brought up between Dublin, London and Sligo, studied painting and then poetry, founded the Irish Literary Society (1892) and the Abbey Theatre (1904) with Lady Gregory, and made his name with The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), The Wind Among the Reeds (1899) and The Green Helmet (1910). He married George Hyde-Lees in 1917, served as a Senator of the Irish Free State (1922–28), won the Nobel Prize in 1923, and died at Roquebrune in the south of France on 28 January 1939, reburied at Drumcliff in 1948.
literary_profile: Yeats is the greatest poet in English of the first half of the twentieth century. He began as a symbolist of the Celtic twilight, made the Abbey Theatre a national institution, and then remade his style three times — into the public, colloquial, bitter poetry of Responsibilities (1914) and The Wild Swans at Coole (1917), the mythic system of A Vision (1925) and the late, bare, terrifying poems of The Tower (1928) and Last Poems. He is the only poet of the period who is equally important as a lyric poet, a dramatist, a prose writer and a public figure.
stylistic_characteristics: The symbolist image and the esoteric system; the rhymed stanza and the refrain refined into bareness; the antithetical rhetoric ('That is no country for old men'); the dramatic mask and the anti-self; the public poem in the grand manner; the prose of a great talker.
intellectual_concerns: Ireland, nationality, and the national question; the heroic past and the mythic cycle; love, the beloved and the ageing body; the occult, the séance, and the system of the gyres; violence, revolution, and the Easter Rising; age, death, and the fury of the old man.
historical_significance: Yeats is the central poet of the period and the founder of the Irish national literature: he created the Abbey Theatre, made Irish myth a modern poetic resource, and wrote the greatest body of lyric poetry in English in the twentieth century. His late poems are among the summit achievements of the language.
